content: Vaccines targeting all stages of the malaria parasite are currently under development, with a primary focus on Plasmodium falciparum, the species responsible for the most severe form of malaria. Pre-erythrocytic vaccines are designed to act on the sporozoite and liver stages of the parasite, aiming to prevent or delay the onset of malaria before the parasite enters the bloodstream. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of pre-erythrocytic malaria vaccines in preventing any form of human malaria. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in March 2006 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and the Science Citation Index. Additional sources such as conference proceedings, reference lists, and direct communication with organizations and researchers were also utilized. The study included randomized controlled trials that compared pre-erythrocytic vaccines with placebo, control vaccines, or standard antimalarial measures. Participants of any age were included, whether they were exposed to malaria through artificial challenge or natural transmission. Trial quality was independently assessed by two authors, and data were extracted for analysis. Meta-analyses were conducted, with results expressed as risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals, using an intention-to-treat approach. The analysis incorporated data from nine trials assessing both safety and efficacy, as well as two trials focused solely on safety, involving over 3,000 participants. Among semi-immune children, the RTS,S vaccine demonstrated a 26% reduction in clinical malaria episodes (95% CI: 13% to 37%) and a 58% reduction in severe malaria cases (95% CI: 15% to 79%) over a period of up to 18 months. Additionally, the prevalence of parasitemia was reduced by 26% (95% CI: 11% to 38%) at six months post-vaccination. In semi-immune adult men, the RTS,S vaccine reduced clinical malaria episodes by 63% (95% CI: 18% to 83%) during the second year of follow-up after a booster dose. No severe adverse events were attributed to the RTS,S vaccine. However, participants in the vaccine group experienced higher frequencies of localized injection site reactions (pain, swelling, and limited arm motion) as well as systemic symptoms such as headache and malaise. In contrast, there was no evidence of efficacy for the CS-NANP vaccines (307 participants across three trials), the CS102 peptide vaccine (14 participants in one trial), or the ME-TRAP vaccine (372 participants in one trial). In conclusion, the RTS,S vaccine was shown to be effective in preventing a significant number of clinical malaria cases, including providing substantial protection against severe malaria in children for up to 18 months. The absence of severe adverse events linked to the vaccine supports its continued development and progression toward licensing, with ongoing efforts to enhance its efficacy. However, other pre-erythrocytic vaccines evaluated in this study did not demonstrate promising results, underscoring the need for further research in this area.
